mcqs.q: Regarding the level of an information resource:
opts: The highest resource is not always the best; the best source matches your question and is current, credible and applicable
The highest resource is always the best available evidence
Tertiary sources should never be used in medicine
Primary sources are always preferable to secondary sources
mcqs.explain: The best source is the one that matches your question, is current, credible, and applicable to your patient or research topic.

mcqs.q: A primary source is one in which:
opts: The researchers report their own original study
Authors analyze, compare or combine other studies
Information from many sources is summarized
A clinical guideline is issued by a professional body
mcqs.explain: Examples are RCTs, cohort studies, qualitative interviews, surveys, laboratory studies and case reports.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a PRIMARY source?
opts: A randomized controlled trial
A systematic review
A meta-analysis
A textbook chapter
mcqs.explain: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are secondary; textbooks are tertiary.

mcqs.q: A secondary source is one in which:
opts: Authors analyze, compare, or combine primary studies
The researchers report their own original data
Information is summarized from many sources for quick reference
A single patient's case is described
mcqs.explain: Examples are systematic reviews, meta-analyses, evidence-based guidelines and critically appraised topics.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a SECONDARY source?
opts: An evidence-based clinical guideline
A cohort study
A drug reference handbook
A case report
mcqs.explain: Cohort studies and case reports are primary; drug references are tertiary.

mcqs.q: Textbooks, encyclopedias, clinical handbooks and drug references are:
opts: Tertiary sources
Primary sources
Secondary sources
Grey literature
mcqs.explain: Tertiary sources summarize information from many sources.

mcqs.q: A case report is classified as:
opts: A primary source
A secondary source
A tertiary source
Not an information resource
mcqs.explain: The researchers report their own original observation.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a stated reason for managing references?
opts: To increase the number of citations your paper receives
To prevent loss of important articles and notes
To ensure accurate and consistent in-text citations and reference lists
To support collaboration and sharing within research teams
mcqs.explain: The three stated reasons concern retention, accuracy and collaboration.

mcqs.q: A reference-management program is software that:
opts: Stores bibliographic details, organizes references, and supports multiple citation styles
Checks papers for plagiarism
Performs the statistical analysis of a study
Searches PubMed using MeSH terms automatically
mcqs.explain: Bibliographic details include author, title, journal and year.

mcqs.q: Which three are named as common reference-management tools?
opts: Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote
Elicit, Consensus, Scite
Rayyan, SciSpace, Litmaps
PubMed, Embase, Scopus
mcqs.explain: The second and third groups are AI tools; the fourth are databases.

mcqs.q: A citation style is:
opts: A set of rules for formatting in-text citations and reference lists
A method of ranking journals by impact
A rule for how many references a paper must have
A plagiarism-detection algorithm
mcqs.explain: It ensures consistency and helps readers locate sources; different disciplines and journals use different styles.

mcqs.q: Which citation style is numeric?
opts: Vancouver
Harvard
APA
All three are numeric
mcqs.explain: Harvard and APA are author–date styles.

mcqs.q: In Vancouver style, in-text citations appear as:
opts: Numbers in brackets or superscript, in order of first mention
Author surname and year
Full references in footnotes
Author surname only
mcqs.explain: The reference list is numbered in the same order as the citations.

mcqs.q: In Vancouver style, the reference list is ordered:
opts: Numerically, in the same order as the citations
Alphabetically by author surname
Chronologically by publication year
Alphabetically by journal title
mcqs.explain: Vancouver is widely used in biomedical and clinical journals.

mcqs.q: The typical Vancouver journal article format is:
opts: Author(s). Title. Journal. Year;Volume(Issue):Pages.
Author, A. A. (Year). Title. Journal, volume(issue), pages.
Author(s) (Year) ‘Title’, Journal, volume(issue), pp. pages.
Title. Author(s). Journal, Year.
mcqs.explain: The second option is APA and the third is Harvard.

mcqs.q: APA and Harvard are described as:
opts: Author–date styles
Numeric styles
Footnote styles
Styles used only in the biomedical sciences
mcqs.explain: In both, the in-text citation gives the author and year.

mcqs.q: In APA and Harvard styles, the reference list is ordered:
opts: Alphabetically by author surname
Numerically by order of citation
By journal title
By publication year, newest first
mcqs.explain: The in-text citation gives the author and year, for example (Ali, 2025).

mcqs.q: The APA journal article format is:
opts: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of article. Title of Journal, volume(issue), pages. https://doi.org/…
Author(s). Title. Journal. Year;Volume(Issue):Pages.
Author(s) (Year) ‘Title’, Journal, volume(issue), pp. pages.
Journal, Year. Author(s), Title.
mcqs.explain: The second is Vancouver and the third is the Harvard pattern.

mcqs.q: “Smith J, Ahmed R. The role of physical activity in preventing cardiovascular disease. J Fam Med. 2024;15(2):120-128.” is written in:
opts: Vancouver style
Harvard style
APA style
No recognized style
mcqs.explain: The abbreviated journal title and the semicolon before the volume are the Vancouver signatures.

mcqs.q: “Smith, J. and Ahmed, R. (2024) ‘The role of physical activity in preventing cardiovascular disease’, Journal of Family Medicine, 15(2), pp. 120–128.” is written in:
opts: Harvard style
Vancouver style
APA style
MLA style
mcqs.explain: The year in parentheses after the authors, the quoted article title, the full journal name and pp. before the pages are Harvard features.

mcqs.q: A student uses Vancouver style. The correct approach is:
opts: In-text superscript number or number in brackets; reference list ordered by number of first citation
In-text (Ali, 2025); reference list ordered alphabetically
In-text author and year in the sentence; reference list ordered by year
In-text footnote with the full reference and no reference list
mcqs.explain: Vancouver numbers citations in the order of first mention and numbers the reference list the same way.

mcqs.q: A student uses Harvard style. The correct approach is:
opts: In-text author surname and year; reference list ordered alphabetically by author
In-text numbers in brackets; reference list ordered numerically
In-text full reference in a footnote; no reference list
In-text only the year; reference list ordered by journal title
mcqs.explain: Harvard is an author–date style with an alphabetical reference list.

mcqs.q: Plagiarism is defined as:
opts: Using someone else's ideas, words, data, or work without proper acknowledgment
Copying text word for word only
Publishing in a predatory journal
Failing to obtain ethical approval
mcqs.explain: It covers ideas and data as well as words.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed as a form of plagiarism?
opts: Citing a source you have read but disagree with
Copying text without quotation marks or citation
Paraphrasing too closely without citation
Using figures, tables, or data without permission and citation
mcqs.explain: Reusing your own previous work without citation, or self-plagiarism, is the fourth listed form.

mcqs.q: Reusing your own previous work without citation is called:
opts: Self-plagiarism
Duplicate authorship
Falsification
Selective reporting
mcqs.explain: It is explicitly included under plagiarism.

mcqs.q: The correct way to paraphrase is to:
opts: Read, understand, set aside the source, then write in your own words — and still cite the original idea
Change a few words in each sentence and cite the source
Rewrite the sentence in a different order without citing it
Translate the passage into another language
mcqs.explain: Paraphrasing too closely without citation is itself a form of plagiarism.

mcqs.q: The advice given for uncertain cases is:
opts: When in doubt, over-cite rather than under-cite
When in doubt, leave the citation out
When in doubt, quote the passage in full
When in doubt, ask the original author for permission
mcqs.explain: Other measures include taking clear notes with full source details and using a reference manager.

mcqs.q: Predatory journals are those that:
opts: Prioritize publication fees over rigorous peer review and editorial standards
Charge no fees but reject most submissions
Publish only systematic reviews
Are indexed only in Google Scholar
mcqs.explain: They may mislead authors about indexing, impact factors or editorial boards, and publishing in them can damage credibility and waste effort.

mcqs.q: The core principle for using AI in literature reviews is:
opts: Use AI to support your thinking, not to replace your critical reading, analysis, or writing
Use AI for the search but never for summarizing
Use AI only if the IRB has approved it
Use AI only for systematic reviews
mcqs.explain: AI must be used responsibly and ethically, with human oversight and verification.

mcqs.q: In the discovery and search stage, AI tools can:
opts: Suggest keywords, identify related papers, and rank papers by relevance
Decide which papers to include without human checking
Replace the need to search PubMed
Guarantee complete coverage of the literature
mcqs.explain: Named examples are Elicit, Consensus, ResearchRabbit, Litmaps, Connected Papers and Scite.

mcqs.q: AI summarization of individual papers helps you quickly understand:
opts: The research question and methods, key findings and conclusions, and strengths and limitations
Only the abstract of the paper
The impact factor of the journal
Whether the study had ethical approval
mcqs.explain: Named examples are SciSpace, Scite and Elicit.

mcqs.q: AI-enhanced reference managers can help you:
opts: Tag and categorize papers by theme and generate bibliographies in different citation styles
Write the discussion section of your review
Decide the inclusion criteria for a systematic review
Verify that each reference actually exists
mcqs.explain: Named examples are Zotero with AI plugins, Mendeley and EndNote.

mcqs.q: For systematic reviews, AI can assist with screening and data extraction by:
opts: Prioritizing papers for screening and suggesting inclusion or exclusion decisions, with human verification
Making final inclusion decisions without human input
Writing the protocol independently
Assigning quality scores that need no checking
mcqs.explain: Named examples are Rayyan for AI-assisted screening and Elicit for data extraction.

mcqs.q: AI hallucination in a literature review means that:
opts: AI may invent references that do not exist or misattribute findings
AI produces summaries that are too long
AI ranks irrelevant papers highly
AI cannot access subscription journals
mcqs.explain: The remedy is to verify every citation in PubMed or your library database and read the original paper before citing.

mcqs.q: The limitation of incomplete coverage means AI tools may miss:
opts: Older papers, non-English articles, or grey literature
Only papers published in the last year
Only randomized controlled trials
Only papers with no abstract
mcqs.explain: The remedy is to use traditional databases such as PubMed, Embase and Cochrane in addition to AI tools.

mcqs.q: The limitation described as “no true synthesis” means AI cannot:
opts: Develop thematic frameworks, identify research gaps, or create analytical connections between sources
Summarize a single paper
Suggest search keywords
Format a bibliography
mcqs.explain: You must personally synthesize the literature and develop your own critical analysis.

mcqs.q: The remedy for AI's outdated knowledge is to:
opts: Check publication dates and search for recent papers manually
Use a different AI model
Restrict the search to review articles
Avoid AI entirely
mcqs.explain: AI models have knowledge cutoffs and may not include the most recent studies.

mcqs.q: Regarding accountability for a literature review:
opts: The researcher is fully accountable for everything in it; AI cannot take responsibility
The AI vendor is responsible for factual errors
Responsibility is shared between the researcher and the AI tool
The journal is responsible once the paper is accepted
mcqs.explain: AI cannot take responsibility for accuracy, completeness, or ethical use of information.

mcqs.q: A student finds that an AI tool has produced a reference they cannot locate in PubMed. They should:
opts: Remove or verify it — an unverifiable reference is a hallucination and must not be cited
Cite it anyway since the AI generated it
Cite it but mark it as AI-generated
Replace the journal name with a real one
mcqs.explain: Every citation must be verified in PubMed or a library database, and the original paper read before citing.

mcqs.q: Which combination correctly pairs a source with its level?
opts: Meta-analysis — secondary; survey — primary; encyclopedia — tertiary
Meta-analysis — primary; survey — secondary; encyclopedia — tertiary
Meta-analysis — tertiary; survey — primary; encyclopedia — secondary
Meta-analysis — secondary; survey — tertiary; encyclopedia — primary
mcqs.explain: Meta-analyses combine primary studies; surveys report original data; encyclopedias summarize many sources.

saqs.q: Describe primary, secondary and tertiary information resources with examples, and state which resource is best.
saqs.a: Medical information resources are the places where you can find evidence for assignments, literature reviews and clinical questions. Primary sources are those in which the researchers report their own original study; examples are randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, qualitative interviews, surveys, laboratory studies and case reports. Secondary sources are those in which authors analyze, compare or combine primary studies; examples are systematic reviews, meta-analyses, evidence-based guidelines and critically appraised topics. Tertiary sources are resources that summarize information from many sources; examples are textbooks, encyclopedias, clinical handbooks, drug references and many clinical databases. Importantly, the highest resource is not always the best resource: the best source is the one that matches your question, is current, credible, and applicable to your patient or research topic.

saqs.q: Explain why references are managed and what a reference-management program does.
saqs.a: References are managed to prevent loss of important articles and notes, to ensure accurate and consistent in-text citations and reference lists, and to support collaboration and sharing within research teams. A reference-management program is software that stores bibliographic details such as author, title, journal and year, organizes references, and supports multiple citation styles including APA, Vancouver and Harvard. Common tools are Zotero, Mendeley and EndNote.

saqs.q: Compare the Vancouver, Harvard and APA citation styles.
saqs.a: A citation style is a set of rules for formatting in-text citations and reference lists; it ensures consistency and helps readers locate sources, and different disciplines and journals use different styles. Vancouver is numeric: in the text, numbers appear in brackets or as superscript in the order of first mention, for example Diabetes is common with a superscript one, and the reference list is numbered in the same order as the citations. Its typical journal article format is Author(s). Title. Journal. Year;Volume(Issue):Pages, and it is widely used in biomedical and clinical journals. APA and Harvard are author-date styles: in the text the author and year are given, for example (Ali, 2025) or Ali (2025) reported, and the reference list is alphabetical by author surname. The APA journal article format is Author, A. A. (Year). Title of article. Title of Journal, volume(issue), pages, followed by the DOI. Harvard uses a similar author-date format with small variations. For example, the same article appears in Vancouver as Smith J, Ahmed R. The role of physical activity in preventing cardiovascular disease. J Fam Med. 2024;15(2):120-128, and in Harvard as Smith, J. and Ahmed, R. (2024) The role of physical activity in preventing cardiovascular disease, Journal of Family Medicine, 15(2), pp. 120-128.

saqs.q: Define plagiarism, list its forms, and explain how to avoid it.
saqs.a: Plagiarism is using someone else's ideas, words, data, or work without proper acknowledgment. It includes copying text without quotation marks or citation; paraphrasing too closely without citation; using figures, tables, or data without permission and citation; and reusing your own previous work without citation, which is self-plagiarism. To avoid it, take clear notes and always record full source details; use quotation marks for exact wording and cite immediately; paraphrase properly by reading, understanding, setting aside the source and then writing in your own words, while still citing the original idea even when paraphrased; use a reference manager to insert citations consistently; check your work with plagiarism-detection tools if available; and when in doubt, over-cite rather than under-cite.

saqs.q: What are predatory journals and why do they matter?
saqs.a: Predatory journals are journals that prioritize publication fees over rigorous peer review and editorial standards. They may mislead authors about indexing, impact factors, or editorial boards. Publishing in such journals can damage credibility and waste effort, because the value of a legitimate journal comes from the rigour of its review whereas a predatory journal's income comes from accepting as many papers as possible.

saqs.q: Describe how AI tools can assist a literature review and list their limitations.
saqs.a: Artificial intelligence tools can help you search, organize and understand the literature more efficiently, but they must be used responsibly and ethically, with human oversight and verification; the core principle is to use AI to support your thinking, not to replace your critical reading, analysis or writing. In discovery and search, AI can suggest keywords and search terms based on your research question, identify related papers, and rank papers by relevance, using tools such as Elicit, Consensus, ResearchRabbit, Litmaps, Connected Papers and Scite. In summarization, AI can generate summaries of individual papers covering the research question and methods, key findings and conclusions, and strengths and limitations, using tools such as SciSpace, Scite and Elicit. In organization and reference management, AI-enhanced managers can tag and categorize papers by theme or topic and generate bibliographies in different citation styles, using Zotero with AI plugins, Mendeley and EndNote. For systematic reviews, AI can assist with screening and data extraction by prioritizing papers for screening based on relevance, suggesting inclusion and exclusion decisions with human verification, and extracting data fields such as study design, sample size and outcomes, using tools such as Rayyan and Elicit. The limitations are hallucinations, in which AI invents references that do not exist or misattributes findings, so every citation must be verified in PubMed or a library database and the original paper read before citing; incomplete coverage, since AI tools may miss important studies especially older papers, non-English articles or grey literature, so traditional databases such as PubMed, Embase and Cochrane must also be used; no true synthesis, since AI cannot develop thematic frameworks, identify research gaps or create analytical connections between sources, so you must personally synthesize the literature and develop your own critical analysis; outdated knowledge, since AI models have knowledge cutoffs and may not include the most recent studies, so publication dates must be checked and recent papers searched manually; and no accountability, since AI cannot take responsibility for accuracy, completeness or ethical use of information, so you are fully accountable for everything in your literature review.
